_comment: Michael Dickens, "Where I Am Donating in 2026", snapshotted by scripts/fetch-mdickens-reviews.ts. Each body opens with his classification of the org, then his write-up, then his top-five prioritization note or donation reasoning where there is one.

reviews.review:
Classification: Favorite donation target; donating $55,000

[Evitable](https://evitable.com/) is a new org that does public advocacy for a global moratorium on ASI. They do grassroots organizing—they’ve been involved in protests and done some preliminary movement-building, and they plan to do more kinds of mobilization in the future. They also make public content on AI risk, including appearing in [various national news outlets](https://evitable.com/in-the-news).

A big component of my decision process is: find writings (or interviews, etc.) by the leader of an org and see how reasonable they sound. Do they understand the AI risk situation? Do they understand why alignment is hard? Are they focusing on the right things? Evitable gets big points because their founder David Krueger scores exceptionally well on the reasonableness test. I read some of his news articles and [LessWrong posts](http://lesswrong.com/users/david-scott-krueger) and found myself cheering along with everything he said.

Evitable has more expertise on AI and AI alignment than the other grassroots advocacy orgs—[David Krueger](https://davidscottkrueger.com/) is an Assistant Professor in Machine Learning and has [co-authored](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=5Uz70IoAAAAJ) numerous AI safety papers; he and Gretchen Krueger (also at Evitable) are co-authors on the recent paper [The Feasibility of a Hardwired Pause of Frontier AI Training](https://hardwired-pause.ai/). This sort of expertise isn’t a requirement for running an advocacy org, but it’s a nice bonus.

Evitable hasn’t done much yet. I talked to them about their plans, and I’m reasonably confident that they will make good tradeoffs about what directions to pursue. A downside of their approach (focusing on capacity-building first) is that AI timelines may be very short, and their efforts might not pay off in time.

I’m still unsure what sort of work to prioritize, but I lean toward public-focused pause advocacy and grassroots organizing.

Last year, I [donated to PauseAI US](https://mdickens.me/2025/11/22/where_i_am_donating_in_2025/#where-im-donating). I wrote: “PauseAI US is serving some important functions that nobody else is on top of.” That’s not true anymore. Evitable, People for a Pause, and Stop the AI Race now exist in the same space as PauseAI US; I’m somewhat more optimistic about their ability to succeed (and especially to form coalitions with others in AI safety).

Out of the advocacy orgs on my list, I have the most trust in Evitable’s leadership in terms of their ability to understand AI risk, think clearly, and prioritize the right things. In terms of competence at execution, Evitable doesn’t stand out as clearly the best, but they don’t look worse either, so the understanding/thinking/prioritization is the decisive factor for me.

**This year, I am donating $55,000 to Evitable.**

reviews.review:
Classification: Tax-deductible; on my short list, but I prefer public advocacy

[Lightcone Infrastructure](https://www.lightconeinfrastructure.com/) takes AI risk seriously, and they do various projects that they expect to improve the situation. They mainly build community support and infrastructure, including running LessWrong, the Lighthaven event venue, and (more recently) creating the philanthropy platform [Lightcone Commons](https://www.lightconecommons.com/).

Lightcone leadership is strategically and organizationally competent. The org is good enough to make my short list, but it’s difficult to weigh the marginal value of community infrastructure against more direct public advocacy. My vibe sense is I prefer advocacy.

There’s a conflict of interest in that I was paid by Lightcone Infrastructure to do some work this year, but at that point I was already pretty sure I wasn’t going to donate to them.

reviews.classification: Tax-deductible; on my short list, but less funding-constrained than the others
reviews.review:
Classification: Tax-deductible; on my short list, but less funding-constrained than the others

If MIRI had no money, it would be a *strong* contender for the best place to donate. However, the other orgs on my list are funding-constrained to a degree that MIRI isn’t. I really, really want Nate Soares and Eliezer Yudkowsky to keep raising the alarm about AI risk, but there is no danger that MIRI runs out of money and they stop being able to do that. The *marginal* things MIRI can do with funding are still good, but probably not as good as some of the other orgs on my short list.

Classification: Tax-deductible; the org I was second most likely to donate to

[Palisade](http://palisaderesearch.org/) isn’t my 2nd favorite org on this list, but it’s the one where I was 2nd most likely to donate—I liked Evitable more than the other grassroots advocacy orgs, Palisade is doing something different (see [my 2024 summary](https://mdickens.me/2024/11/18/where_i_am_donating_in_2024/#palisade-research)), and I was uncertain about which approach was better. I decided I still prefer to donate to grassroots advocacy, the same as in 2024 and 2025.

The main update on Palisade is that in 2024, they had mostly done technical work and were just starting to scale up their political advocacy. Now, in 2026, they have been actively doing political advocacy, and I like what I’ve seen from them (although I don’t know a lot of details).

reviews.review:
Classification: Tax-deductible; I support their work, but prefer US-based orgs

[PauseAI Global](https://pauseai.info/) organizes protests outside of the US. As I wrote in [2024](https://mdickens.me/2024/11/18/where_i_am_donating_in_2024/#pauseai-global), I support their work, but I prefer to donate to US-based orgs because I believe US AI policy matters much more than policy in any other country.

As of November 2026, their website directs US readers to [People for a Pause](https://peopleforapause.org/). This suggests that, if I like PauseAI Global, I should donate to People for a Pause. I decided not to donate to People for a Pause because I know more about Evitable and Stop the AI Race and I trust the latter orgs more.

I have two concerns about PauseAI Global based on private information. The first is a minor concern that I know to be true; the second is a medium-to-large concern, but I don’t know whether it’s accurate. I would prefer not to make vague statements like this, but unfortunately that is the situation. I would probably still donate to PauseAI Global if they were the only org doing protests.

reviews.review:
Classification: Tax-deductible; this year I’d rather donate to Evitable or Stop the AI Race

I talked about why I liked PauseAI US in [2024](https://mdickens.me/2024/11/18/where_i_am_donating_in_2024/#pauseai-us) and [2025](https://mdickens.me/2025/11/22/where_i_am_donating_in_2025/#where-im-donating). One positive update is that PauseAI US now spends more time coordinating volunteers’ meetings with policy-makers across the country, which is a great thing to do.

A lot of people in AI safety take issue with the fact that PauseAI US’s director, Holly Elmore, behaves antagonistically toward many people on Twitter, especially AI company employees. I don’t spiritually object to this. Most safety work at AI companies is safetywashing, papering over misalignment, or contributing more to capabilities than to safety; the people doing those things should stop. That doesn’t necessarily mean you should call them out personally in public. I’m not overly concerned that Holly is violating some important norm; if anyone’s violating norms, it’s the people working at AI companies. I’ve heard some accuse Holly of dishonesty, but the statements being pointed to as dishonest strike me as more like biased or motivated. ([Here](https://x.com/MichaelJDickens/status/2099557611079340246) is my Twitter reply to one specific claim.)

Sometimes Holly criticizes AI safety people who (in my view) are doing good work, but have associations with AI companies. I think that’s going too far, although I see where she’s coming from.

I *am* concerned that many people dislike Holly’s Twitter presence. It creates two problems:

- It gives many people a bad impression of the AI pause movement.
- It makes some other orgs unwilling to work with PauseAI US, which makes cooperation harder—this is important for organizing protests, etc.

Is it strategically useful to be antagonistic on Twitter? [Holly says yes](https://hollyelmore.substack.com/p/on-callouts); I lean toward no, although I don’t have a strong view.

Last year, I was concerned about the downside risk, but I believed it was outweighed by PauseAI US’s activities on things I liked: protests, messaging campaigns, organizing meetings between policy-makers and concerned citizens. And there wasn’t anyone else doing all those things. I have become more concerned about the downside risk since then, and there are more people organizing protests and grassroots support than there were a year ago. Therefore, this year I’d rather donate to Evitable or Stop the AI Race, although I still believe the more extreme criticisms of PauseAI US are overstated.

reviews.review:
Classification: Tax-deductible; a strong candidate, but I trust Evitable more

[Stop the AI Race](https://stoptherace.ai/) It co-organized a [large SF protest](https://luma.com/s0k8wvee) earlier this year. Before that, the org’s founder, Michaël Trazzi, [did a hunger strike against DeepMind](https://b17news.com/im-on-a-hunger-strike-outside-deepminds-office-in-london-heres-what-i-fear-most-about-ai/). I’m impressed by his agency and dedication, and I like what I’ve seen so far.

There isn’t much info available about Stop the AI Race. Even though the org is a strong candidate, I decided not to investigate further because I wasn’t sure what information would convince me to donate. It comes down to who I trust more to execute well; Stop the AI Race looks promising on that front, but right now I trust Evitable more, and I don’t know how to get good information other than just waiting and seeing who gets more traction.
